---
title: The Dollar Sign
---

The last chapter ended on an idea worth carrying into this one: the shell
rewrites your line before the command runs. `*.txt` never reaches `ls`. The
shell replaces it with the names it matched, and `ls` sees an ordinary list of
files.

A wildcard is one rewrite of that kind. This chapter is about another, and it
is the one you will reach for most often. It is marked by a `$`.

There are three of them:

* `$name` - the value of a variable
* `$(command)` - the output of running a command
* `$((...))` - the result of a calculation

They look alike because they are alike. In each case the shell works something
out and drops the answer into your line, before the command starts. No new
commands are needed here - `echo` and `date` will do.

## The dollar you do not type

Before anything else, a `$` you have been looking at since the first chapter,
and a `$` that is new.

```session
$ echo $HOME
/home/anand
```

There are two dollar signs on that line, and they have nothing to do with each
other.

The first one is the **prompt**. The shell prints it to say it is ready. You
never type it, and it is not part of the command.

The second one is yours. You typed it, and it asks the shell for the value of
`HOME`.

Telling them apart is easier than it sounds: the prompt is always the first
thing on the line, with a space after it. Every other `$` on the line is one
you typed.

::: {.callout-tip}
When you copy an example from these notes, leave the leading `$` behind. Copy
`echo $HOME`, not `$ echo $HOME`.
:::

We said earlier that a `$` in an example means "this is a command you type".
That was the `$` at the start of the line. From here on the character has a
second job, and the rest of this chapter is about that one.

## Variables

The shell can keep a value under a name. A name with a value under it is called
a **variable**, and you can make your own.

To store a value, write a name, an `=`, and the value:

```session
$ name=alice
```

Nothing is printed. Storing a value is quiet work, like `cd` and `touch`.

To get the value back, put a `$` in front of the name:

```session
$ echo $name
alice
```

Look at what happened there. `echo` prints the arguments it is given, and it
printed `alice` - so `alice` must have been its argument. `echo` never saw
`$name` at all. The shell replaced it first, and the command that actually ran
was:

```
echo alice
```

This is the same rewriting that `*` does, with a different way of working out
the answer.

It is called a variable because the value can vary. Set it again and the old
value is gone:

```session
$ name=bob
```

```session
$ echo $name
bob
```

## Watch the spaces

There is one rule to get right, and it catches everybody once:

```session
$ name = alice
bash: name: command not found
```

With spaces around the `=`, the shell reads the line the way it reads every
other line: a command called `name`, given the arguments `=` and `alice`. There
is no such command.

::: {.callout-warning}
No spaces around the `=`. Write `name=alice`, not `name = alice`.
:::

Asking for a name you never set is not an error either:

```session
$ echo $city
```

The shell replaces `$city` with nothing at all, and `echo` prints an empty
line. This is worth remembering. A misspelled name does not complain - it
quietly turns into nothing, and the command runs anyway.

## Variables the shell already has

Some variables are set up for you when you log in. `USER` holds your login
name:

```session
$ echo $USER
anand
```

And `HOME` holds the path to your home directory:

```session
$ echo $HOME
/home/anand
```

There are quite a few of these, and they are how the system tells every program
about your account and your settings. We will come back to the whole collection
later, when we look at what a script inherits from the shell that started it.

::: {.callout-tip}
The shell's own variables are spelled in capitals. Keeping your own in
lowercase - `name`, `today`, `count` - means you will never accidentally
overwrite one of them.
:::

## The output of a command

The second form runs a command and hands you what it printed. Write the command
inside `$(...)`:

```session
$ echo "Today is $(date)"
Today is Wed Sep  9 10:12:43 IST 2026
```

The shell ran `date`, collected the line it printed, and put that line into the
argument it gave `echo`.

This is more useful than it first looks, because the output can be dropped into
the middle of something else. `date` will print just the day if you ask it to:

```session
$ date +%F
2026-09-09
```

So we can build a file name with today's date in it:

```session
$ echo notes-$(date +%F).txt
notes-2026-09-09.txt
```

Nothing was created there. `echo` only printed the name the shell built out of
the pieces. But that is a name you could hand to `cp`, and tomorrow the same
line would build `notes-2026-09-10.txt` without anyone thinking about it.

This is the habit from the last chapter again: put `echo` in front of something
and look at what the shell made of it.

The output of a command can be stored in a variable, like any other value:

```session
$ today=$(date +%F)
```

```session
$ echo $today
2026-09-09
```

## Doing arithmetic

The shell does not do sums by accident. Ask `echo` to add two numbers and it
does what it always does - prints its arguments:

```session
$ echo 2 + 3
2 + 3
```

To get an answer, put the sum inside `$((...))`:

```session
$ echo $((2 + 3))
5
```

Variables work inside it, and here you do not need the `$` on their names -
inside `$((...))` a bare name is understood to be a variable:

```session
$ x=5
```

```session
$ y=2
```

```session
$ echo $((x + y))
7
```

```session
$ echo $((x * y))
10
```

::: {.callout-note}
Shell arithmetic works in whole numbers only. `$((7 / 2))` is `3`, not `3.5` -
the remainder is dropped rather than rounded. For anything else you will want a
proper calculator, and we will meet one later.
:::

## Summary

| What you write | What it means |
|----------------|---------------|
| `x=5` | sets the variable `x` to `5` |
| `x = 5` | an error - no spaces around the `=` |
| `$x` | the value of the variable `x` |
| `$nosuchname` | nothing at all - an unset variable is not an error |
| `$USER` | your login name |
| `$HOME` | the path to your home directory |
| `$(date)` | the output of running `date` |
| `d=$(date)` | sets `d` to the output of `date` |
| `notes-$(date +%F).txt` | `notes-2026-09-09.txt` |
| `$((2 + 3))` | `5` |
| `$((x * y))` | the product of `x` and `y` - no `$` needed on names here |

And the one idea to carry forward: a `$` tells the shell to work something out
and put the answer in its place, before the command runs. The command itself
never sees the `$`.
